subtype: Selling with fake reviews and testimonials [Observer]
passage:
"Salma, come look at this. Ammi wants this water purifier. Four point nine stars."
"So order it, Samir bhai."
"Wait. Read these. 'Best purifier, changed my life, highly recommend to all.' Next one: 'Best purifier, changed my life, highly recommend.' And the next."
"Same sentence, again and again?"
"Two hundred reviews and not one complaint. Not even about delivery. Even my phone has complaints."
"Sort by three stars."
"...Here. 'Works, but the filter needs changing every two months and costs a lot.' 'Service man came after ten days.' These sound like people."
"And all the five-star ones are from the same week in March."
"Let me search the model name on that consumer forum you use."
"Anything?"
"Mixed. Some like it. Some say the filter price is the whole trick."
"So we tell Ammi the truth, and look at two more before buying."
"Yes. And we stop trusting a wall of perfect."

qa.q: How many reviews did Samir count on the page?
qa.a: Samir counted two hundred reviews and not one complaint.

qa.q: What made Samir suspicious of the four point nine rating?
qa.a: Samir doubted the rating because the reviews repeated the same sentence and had no complaints at all, which felt unreal compared with ordinary products.

qa.q: Which checking steps helped Samir and Salma most?
qa.a: Sorting by three stars, noticing the five-star reviews all came in one week, and searching the model on an independent forum gave a truer picture.

qa.q: How might Ammi be affected if they had ordered without checking?
qa.a: Ammi might have been stuck with costly filters and slow service, trusting a purchase her children made on the strength of copied praise.

grounding: Samir notices a product page with identical glowing reviews and no complaints, and he and Salma read middle ratings and an independent forum instead.

passage:
When we moved Jahnavi's things to Pune last October, I was the one who found the packers.
The first company looked perfect online. Forty-two reviews, all five stars. "Very professional team, very careful handling, highly satisfied." I scrolled for a while before it bothered me. Almost every review used the words "very careful handling". Several were posted on the same two days. Nobody mentioned a broken plate, a late truck, anything.
Every real service I've ever used has at least one grumpy customer.
So I opened the same company on a map listing, where anyone can post, and went straight to the three-star and two-star reviews. Two people said the final bill was nearly double the quote.
I chose a smaller firm with a 4.2 and a few honest complaints about being slow. They were slow. Nothing broke.
Jagdish

qa.q: Which words did almost every review of the first company use?
qa.a: Almost every review used the words "very careful handling".

qa.q: Why did the perfect reviews start to bother Jagdish?
qa.a: Jagdish felt uneasy because real services always have some unhappy customers, and these reviews had identical phrases, clustered dates and no complaints.

qa.q: Which step revealed the problem with the first company?
qa.a: Checking the same company on an open map listing and reading the two- and three-star reviews showed bills nearly double the quote.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi have been affected if Jagdish had trusted the first page?
qa.a: Jahnavi could have faced a much higher bill during an already stressful move, based on praise that was not real.

grounding: Jagdish notices a packers' page with only glowing, identically worded reviews and uses middle-rated reviews on an independent listing to choose.

passage:
You're looking at that forward about the other school, Elizabeth. Let me tell you what I did as a schoolgirl of sixteen.
We had phones with tiny screens then, only messages. One evening a text came: "St. Anne's got the quiz questions early. Their captain's uncle is a judge." We had lost to St. Anne's that week. I was so angry my hands shook. It felt true because we already felt cheated.
I didn't ask who wrote it. I sent it to twenty-three people. Sending it felt like standing up for my team.
By Monday it was everywhere. Their captain, a quiet girl called Rosalind, stopped coming to the inter-school events. Her uncle was not a judge. Nobody had checked.
I wrote her a note in December. She never answered. I don't blame her.
That's all, beta. Now tell me, who wrote the one on your phone?
Vidya

qa.q: How many people did young Vidya send the message to?
qa.a: Vidya sent it to twenty-three people.

qa.q: Why did the message feel true to sixteen-year-old Vidya?
qa.a: Vidya was already angry about losing to St. Anne's, so a story that said they had cheated matched what she felt, and forwarding it felt like loyalty.

qa.q: At which point in the story could young Vidya have stopped the harm?
qa.a: When the text arrived, she could have asked who wrote it and whether the uncle was really a judge before sending it to anyone.

qa.q: What was it like for Rosalind once the message spread?
qa.a: Rosalind was blamed for something untrue and stopped coming to inter-school events, so the forward cost her a place she used to enjoy.

grounding: A woman recalls forwarding, at sixteen, an angry rumour about a rival school's captain because it fit what her team already felt.

passage:
It was 10:30 at night, the power had gone, and Mridul's phone was at 9 percent with a maths exam at eight the next morning.
Then the colony cricket group lit up. A blurry photo of their pitch, dug up in patches, and a message: "Green Park boys did this. Share everywhere, everyone should know."
Mridul's face went hot. Green Park had beaten them in the final and laughed about it. Of course it was them. His thumb was already forwarding it to the school group, then the tuition group. He felt like he was protecting his team.
Darshan messaged him privately. "Who took the photo? Whose pitch is that even?"
Mridul looked again by the light of a candle. The fence in the photo was blue. Theirs was green.
His battery hit 4 percent. He deleted the forwards he could and wrote, "Not sure this is our pitch, don't share." Then the screen went dark.

qa.q: What colour was the fence in the photo?
qa.a: The fence in the photo was blue.

qa.q: Why did Mridul forward the photo so fast?
qa.a: Mridul was angry at Green Park for beating his team and laughing, so the message fitted what he already felt and sharing it felt like protecting his side.

qa.q: Which choice helped Mridul stop the rumour, even in a hurry?
qa.a: Looking again after Darshan asked who took the photo, then deleting the forwards and warning others not to share, stopped it before his phone died.

qa.q: What would change for the Green Park boys if Mridul had not looked again?
qa.a: They might have been blamed across several groups for damage they may not have done, just because the story fitted an old rivalry.

grounding: A teenage boy angrily forwards a message blaming a rival team because it fits his group's feelings, then checks the source when questioned.

subtype: Repeated claims begin to feel true [Receiver]
passage:
Week one. Posters went up across the hostel walls in bright red: "Blue Panel sold the hostel fund." Ramesh laughed. "Who writes this stuff?" He voted in college elections only when he remembered.
Week three. The line was in every group chat, on stickers in the canteen, in a song someone played outside the library. Blue Panel's faces were drawn with dollar signs. Over lunch Ramesh heard himself say, "Everyone knows Blue Panel took the money."
Keerthana put down her spoon. "How do you know?"
"It's... everywhere."
"That's not the same as proof. Did anyone show accounts?"
Ramesh opened his mouth and closed it.
Week four. He went to the hostel office and asked for the fund statement. The clerk said it was on the notice board, and had been all along. Ramesh stood reading it for ten minutes, feeling slightly sick at how easily the words had become his own.

qa.q: Where was the fund statement, according to the clerk?
qa.a: The clerk said the fund statement was on the notice board, and had been all along.

qa.q: How did Ramesh feel reading the statement in week four?
qa.a: Ramesh felt slightly sick and uneasy, realising a slogan he had once laughed at had become his own belief without any proof.

qa.q: What turning point made Ramesh go and check?
qa.a: Keerthana asking "How do you know?" and whether anyone had shown accounts made him see that seeing a claim everywhere is not proof.

qa.q: How might Blue Panel's members experience the four weeks of posters?
qa.a: They would be painted as thieves across the campus, with their faces drawn with dollar signs, before anyone asked for evidence.

grounding: Over weeks, a student hears one slogan against a campus panel so often that he repeats it as fact, until asked for proof.

subtype: Repeated claims begin to feel true [Receiver]
passage:
You asked, Ishita, how people believe things with no proof. I was a girl of nineteen, working at the thread mill office in our town, when the new railway quarters filled with families from elsewhere.
Somebody said, "Since they came, things go missing." Then the vegetable seller said it. Then the temple loudspeaker man. Then my own cousin at the mill. Nobody named what went missing. By the monsoon, I said it too, as easily as saying it will rain.
One evening my bicycle chain broke outside those quarters. A girl my age, Kusum, came out with a spanner and fixed it without a word. She had grease to her elbows and a college book under her arm.
Walking home, I tried to remember one thing that had gone missing. I couldn't. I had only heard the same sentence a hundred times.
I stopped saying it after that. Some of my friends didn't.
Lakshmi

qa.q: What did Kusum bring out when Lakshmi's bicycle chain broke?
qa.a: Kusum came out with a spanner and fixed it without a word.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi feeling on the walk home?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt unsettled and ashamed, realising she could not name a single missing thing and had believed a sentence only because she heard it so often.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Lakshmi's story?
qa.a: Meeting Kusum, who helped her, pushed Lakshmi to ask what had actually gone missing, and finding no answer made her stop repeating the claim.

qa.q: How might Kusum's family have lived with the sentence repeated around town?
qa.a: They would have been treated with suspicion by the vegetable seller, the mill and neighbours, blamed for losses nobody could even name.

grounding: A woman recalls how, at nineteen, a claim against newcomers repeated by everyone around her came to feel obvious without any proof.

"Santosh, did you hear about Farida from accounts?"
"Only that she was called to HR on Monday."
"That's not what the floor group says. They say money went missing."

passage:
I watched a rumour nearly cost Suraj his job last winter.
Suraj has been the night watchman in our building for six years. One morning a cycle went missing from the basement. In the Block A group someone wrote, "Watchman was asleep." In Block B it became, "Watchman must know something." By evening the combined group said, "Suraj sold it, obviously," and three people asked the society to change the security agency.
I kept reading the messages and waiting for someone to ask who saw anything. Nobody did. I didn't either, for two whole days.
On the third day, the cycle's owner found it at the repair shop on Station Road. His son had left it there for a puncture.
There was one short message: "Cycle found." No apology.
Suraj still greets everyone at the gate. He doesn't smile at Block A the way he used to.
Deepak

qa.q: Where was the missing cycle found?
qa.a: The cycle was found at the repair shop on Station Road.

qa.q: What does Deepak's admission "I didn't either, for two whole days" suggest Deepak feels now?
qa.a: It suggests Deepak feels regret and some guilt for staying silent while the story grew, even while seeing that nobody had asked for evidence.

qa.a: Someone could have asked who actually saw anything, or spoken to Suraj and the cycle's owner, before the guesses turned into an accusation.

qa.q: How has the rumour affected Suraj, even after the cycle was found?
qa.a: Suraj still does his job, but he no longer smiles at Block A the way he used to, because he was accused without evidence and never received an apology.

grounding: Deepak watches a rumour about a building watchman grow from group to group into an accusation, doing harm before anyone asks who started it.

passage:
Dear Manjula Chechi,
You asked why I didn't forward the message about child-kidnappers in white vans to our family group, when you sent it with three warnings.
Honestly, my first feeling was fear. Anu walks to school. My hand went straight to the forward button.
Then I stopped and asked myself a few things. Who wrote it? There was no name, no place, no date. What did it want me to feel? Scared, and angry at strangers. Who gains if a hundred people panic? Not the children.
I called the local police station's helpline number from their official page. The constable said they had no such reports and that this message had come up in other towns too.
So I didn't send it on. It felt oddly brave, just not pressing a button.
Please do call me before sending the next one. I would rather talk than panic together.
With love,
Yogesh

qa.q: Whom did Yogesh call to check the message?
qa.a: Yogesh called the local police station's helpline number from their official page.

qa.q: What was Yogesh feeling when the message first arrived?
qa.a: Yogesh felt fear for Anu, who walks to school, and Yogesh's hand went straight to the forward button.

qa.q: Which questions helped Yogesh pause before forwarding?
qa.a: Yogesh asked who wrote it, what it was trying to make people feel, and who gains if a hundred people panic, then checked with an official source.

qa.q: How might Manjula Chechi feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Manjula Chechi might feel a little embarrassed, but the warm tone and the invitation to call first make the letter feel caring rather than scolding.

grounding: Yogesh refuses to forward a frightening message after asking who wrote it and why it aims to scare, and checks with an official source instead.

I'm Shalini, Sunaina, and people think fact-checking is only for journalists. For me it looked like a Tuesday at my office.
Someone on my team forwarded a message: "New manager plans to sack everyone over thirty-five. Share before it's deleted." I'm thirty-six. My stomach went cold.
Everybody was forwarding it. I had it copied, ready.
And then I noticed three things. It had no name on it. It wanted me angry and scared at the same time. And "share before it's deleted" is exactly what you say when you don't want people to check.
So I didn't share. I asked HR directly, in writing. They replied the same afternoon: no such plan, and they'd heard the rumour too.
Nobody thanked me, obviously. It isn't the kind of thing people notice. But one colleague said, "You didn't send it? Okay, I'll hold off too."

qa.q: What did HR reply when Shalini asked in writing?
qa.a: HR replied the same afternoon that there was no such plan and that they had heard the rumour too.

qa.q: What was Shalini feeling when the message first arrived?
qa.a: Shalini felt a cold fear, because at thirty-six Shalini was one of the people the message said would be sacked.

qa.q: Which signs made Shalini stop before sharing?
qa.a: The message had no name, tried to stir anger and fear at once, and pushed people to share before it was deleted, which discourages checking.

qa.q: How did Shalini's choice affect the colleague who noticed?
qa.a: Seeing Shalini hold back gave that colleague permission to do the same, so one quiet refusal slowed the rumour further.

grounding: Shalini notices a workplace message is built to stir anger and fear, checks with HR instead of forwarding, and quietly slows the rumour.

passage:
"Thomas, why are you glaring at Ruchika?"
"Santosh, you haven't heard? Voice note in the class group. Her voice, calling the new girl names. Horrible stuff."

passage:
I was fifteen when I saw the video of the famous singer laughing at our town after the floods. It was everywhere. His face, his voice, his usual black kurta. "Those people deserve it," he said, and smirked.
I was furious. Our school had been a shelter for two weeks. I posted a long angry comment and made Samir watch it at recess. "He actually said it, look at his mouth."
Three days later a news channel showed the real clip. He had been talking about a cricket match. Someone had taken his face and voice and made new words come out.
I watched the fake again and saw things I had missed: the lips a little late, the blink that never came. The first time, nobody noticed.
I deleted my comment. Samir said, "It looked real to me too."
What stuck with me was that seeing it had once been enough.
Manoj

qa.q: How long had Manoj's school been a shelter?
qa.a: The school had been a shelter for two weeks.

qa.q: Why was Manoj so ready to believe the video?
qa.a: Manoj was already hurt and angry about the floods, and the video showed the singer's own face and voice, so it felt like proof.

qa.q: What turning point changed Manoj's view of the video?
qa.a: The news channel showing the real clip, about a cricket match, revealed that the face and voice had been used to make new words.

qa.q: How might Samir have felt when Manoj showed the video at recess?
qa.a: Samir was probably pulled into the anger too, and the line "It looked real to me too" shows Samir was just as fooled.

grounding: A teenager believes a fake video of a famous singer because it looks and sounds real, and later learns the medium itself is no longer proof.

subtype: Why people make and share fakes [Observer]
passage:
The tram in Oslo was packed and steamy after the storm. Lars held his phone up to Lindiwe: a shark swimming down a flooded street, right past a bus stop.
"Look at this! Near the harbour!"
Lindiwe tilted her head. "That shark has been in every storm since I was eight. Durban, Houston, now Oslo."
"Why would anyone fake that?"
"Loads of reasons. Some pages make money when you click. Some people want attention. Some fakes are made to make people angry at a politician or scared of a group. Some are just cruel."
"But my aunt shared it."
"Your aunt isn't lying. She shares it because it feels true. The storm was real, so the shark feels possible."
Lars looked at the photo again, calmer now. "So I shouldn't just ask if it's real. I should ask who gets something out of it."
"Exactly. Then you don't need to panic. You just wait."

qa.q: What did the photo on Lars's phone show?
qa.a: It showed a shark swimming down a flooded street, right past a bus stop.

qa.q: How did Lars's feeling change after Lindiwe explained?
qa.a: Lars moved from excitement to calm doubt; he looked at the photo again, calmer, and started thinking about who gains from it.

qa.q: Which question does Lars decide to ask about viral photos from now on?
qa.a: Lars decides to ask who gets something out of a photo, not only whether it is real, so he can doubt calmly instead of panicking.

qa.q: How does Lindiwe see Lars's aunt differently from the person who made the fake?
qa.a: Lindiwe sees the aunt as honest but fooled, sharing because it feels true, while the maker may want money, attention, anger or cruelty.

grounding: On a tram, Lindiwe explains to Lars that fakes are made for clicks, attention, politics or cruelty and shared by people who feel they are true.

subtype: Why people make and share fakes [Observer]
passage:
In the Class 9 computer lab, Simran ma'am pulled up two images on the projector. One was the fake notice that had gone round the week before, saying the school would close for a heatwave. The other was a cruel edited photo of a boy from another school, his face stretched into a pig's snout.
"Both of these were made by someone," she said. "Why?"
Bidisha raised her hand. "For fun?"
"Sometimes. Let's list them." On the board she wrote: money, clicks, politics, cruelty.
"The heatwave notice got a page thousands of new followers. That's clicks. The photo of the boy? Cruelty."
"But Didi forwarded the heatwave one," Bidisha said quietly. "She's not a liar."
"No. Most people who share fakes believe the feeling in them. It was hot. A holiday felt possible."
Bidisha wrote that down. It felt less like being tricked, more like seeing the machine.

qa.q: What four reasons did Simran ma'am write on the board?
qa.a: She wrote money, clicks, politics and cruelty.

qa.q: How did Bidisha feel after hearing why people share fakes?
qa.a: Bidisha felt less foolish and calmer, as if she was seeing how the machine works instead of just being tricked.

qa.q: What makes Simran ma'am's lesson work well?
qa.a: She uses real examples the class has seen, lets students suggest reasons, and separates the makers' motives from the sharers who believe the feeling.

qa.q: How might Bidisha's Didi feel if she heard this lesson?
qa.a: Didi might feel relieved not to be called a liar, and more ready to pause next time because she understands why the notice felt true.

grounding: Simran ma'am explains that fakes are made for money, clicks, politics or cruelty and shared by people who believe the feeling, helping a student doubt calmly.

subtype: Deepfake used to shame or extort [Receiver]
passage:
The message came at 7:10 in the evening, from an account with no photo. A video: Chinmay's own face, at what looked like the college canteen, pushing money from the till into his pocket. Then: "Pay 8000 by midnight or this goes to your class group and your parents."
Chinmay had never touched that till. He sat on the floor of his rented room, heart pounding, already opening his banking app.
He called Hemant instead, his older cousin, before he could change his mind.
Hemant arrived in twenty minutes, still in his office shirt. "This is not your fault. Don't pay, don't reply. Screenshot everything: the video, the account, the time."
They reported the account on the app. Then Hemant drove them to the cyber police station.
The sub-inspector noted every detail. "You did right coming today. Paying only brings a bigger demand. We'll file it now and flag the account."
On the drive back, Chinmay finally cried.

qa.q: How much money did the message demand, and by when?
qa.a: The message demanded 8000 by midnight.

qa.q: What was Chinmay feeling when he first saw the video?
qa.a: Chinmay was terrified and ashamed even though he had done nothing, which is why his heart pounded and he nearly opened his banking app to pay.

qa.q: Which choice turned the evening around for Chinmay?
qa.a: Calling Hemant instead of paying; together they saved screenshots, reported the account, and went to the cyber police station the same night.

qa.q: How does Hemant see what happened to Chinmay?
qa.a: Hemant sees Chinmay as the victim of a crime, not someone who did wrong, which is why he says straight away that it is not his fault.

grounding: A young man is threatened with a fake video for money, and with his cousin he saves evidence, reports the account and goes to the cyber police the same day.

"Swati didi, don't turn the light on. Look at this. Someone made a profile with my name."
"...These are your photos from the college fest. But edited. Made to look indecent."

qa.a: Mummy sits beside Disha, tells her none of it is on her, holds her, and starts the cyber crime complaint with her that same night.

passage:
I sit next to Pema at the design studio, so I saw the whole thing on Thursday.
A video was flying around every group: a bridge collapsing, cars sliding into a river, with the caption "Our Ring Road flyover, just now!!" Three people in our office had already shared it. Someone was crying in the pantry.
Pema didn't share it. She paused it, zoomed in, and said, "Those cars are driving on the left, but look at the signs." Then she dragged a frame into an image search. I watched the results load. The same video, from another country, four years ago.
She checked two local news sites next. Nothing about the flyover. She called the office manager to tell the person in the pantry.
I don't know what she was feeling. She looked calm, maybe a little tired. When I asked, she just said, "If I can't find where it came from, I don't send it."
Rashmi

qa.q: How many people in the office had already shared the video?
qa.a: Three people in the office had already shared it.

qa.q: What might Pema have been thinking when she paused the video?
qa.a: Pema probably doubted the caption because details like the road signs did not fit, although Rashmi admits not knowing exactly what she felt.

qa.q: Which of Pema's steps could anyone copy before sharing?
qa.a: Looking at odd details, searching a frame to find where the video first appeared, and checking whether trusted local news carries the story.

qa.q: How was the person crying in the pantry affected by the fake?
qa.a: That person was frightened by a disaster that had not happened here, and Pema's call to the office manager was a way to calm that fear.

grounding: Rashmi watches Pema check a viral disaster video by searching for its source and trusted outlets, and refuse to share what she cannot verify.

passage:
Monday. A screenshot arrived in Imran's alumni group: a news headline saying his old company was shutting its Chennai office, with a logo that looked right. Shankar had already added, "Told you!!" Imran's thumb hovered over forward to his friends still working there. He stopped. No link, just a picture of a headline.
Wednesday. He searched the exact headline. No news site had it. On the company's own press page, the latest note was about a new Chennai hiring drive. He looked at the screenshot again: the font of the date didn't match the rest.
Friday. The fake had reached forty groups. Shankar messaged him privately. "Did you check that thing? My cousin there was panicking."
"I did. It's not real. There's no source anywhere, and the company says the opposite."
"Should've asked you first."
"Next time just don't send it until someone finds the source."

passage:
I wanted to tell you properly, Ramesh sir, because you asked why I stopped coming to the running club.
When we moved here in June I didn't know anyone. Then some seniors invited me to the Circle. It started with morning runs, and it was brilliant. They knew my name on the first day. Wristbands, a chant before every run, "brother" this, "brother" that. For the first time here I felt like I belonged.
Then it changed. Five a.m. meetings, then weekends. Last week the leader told me my old friends from class "hold me back". And he said, "Don't tell your parents about the Circle yet. They won't get it."
That made my stomach go cold.
You listened to all of it, sir, and you didn't laugh. You said wanting friends was completely normal, and hiding a group from my family was the warning sign. Then you called my mum while I was still sitting here.
Hemant

qa.q: What did the leader say about Hemant's old friends from class?
qa.a: The leader said Hemant's old friends from class "hold me back".

qa.q: Why did the Circle feel so good to Hemant at first?
qa.a: Hemant had moved in June and knew nobody, so being known by name, the chant and being called "brother" gave him a strong feeling of belonging.

qa.q: What was the turning point that made Hemant ask for help?
qa.a: Being told not to tell his parents about the Circle made his stomach go cold, and he recognised the secrecy as a warning and went to Ramesh sir.

qa.q: How does Ramesh sir respond to what Hemant tells him?
qa.a: Ramesh sir listens without laughing, tells Hemant that wanting friends is normal and that hiding a group is the warning sign, and calls Hemant's mum that same day.

grounding: A lonely teenager is drawn into an intense group offering quick friendship and rituals, recognises the danger when told to hide it and cut off others, and tells Ramesh sir.

passage:
Nilesh and I have been in the same hostel wing since Class 8, so I noticed when he changed.
This term he started leaving the common room early for "calls with the group". He wore the same grey thread on his wrist every day. He started saying "the awakened" and "sleepers", and when I asked who the sleepers were, he said, "People like you, Tenzin. No offence."
He laughed differently, sort of far away. He stopped coming to Saturday football. I think he was lonely after his best mate left in April, but I don't know that for sure.
Then last Thursday I saw a message on his screen: "Delete this chat. Your warden must not know."
I went to Mrs D'Souza, our house parent, that evening. She listened, thanked me and said telling was right. Before dinner she sat with Nilesh in her office for a long time, and she called his parents that night.

qa.q: What did the message on Nilesh's screen say?
qa.a: It said, "Delete this chat. Your warden must not know."

qa.q: What does Tenzin think might be behind Nilesh's change, and how sure is Tenzin?
qa.a: Tenzin thinks Nilesh may have been lonely after his best mate left in April, but openly says it is only a guess.

qa.q: Which moment made Tenzin act, and was it the right step?
qa.a: The message telling Nilesh to hide the chat from his warden; taking it to the house parent that same evening was right because secrecy is the warning sign.

qa.q: How does Mrs D'Souza respond once Tenzin tells her?
qa.a: Mrs D'Souza listens, thanks Tenzin, sits with Nilesh in her office before dinner and calls his parents that night.

grounding: Tenzin notices a hostel-mate drawn into a secretive group with rituals and new words, and reports it once the group demands secrecy; the house parent acts the same day.
